Yes. So the empty warning is inside the JSONL branch, reached always. So converting to LOG_WARNING makes it print even without verbose.

Now let me implement.

First logger.h: add LOG_WARNING. Placement next to LOG_VERBOSE. Need `<iostream>` for std::cerr? Actually LOG_VERBOSE already uses std::cerr with only ostream/fstream includes. To be safe and conventional, add `<iostream> // std::cerr`. But the include block currently:
```
#include <fstream> // std::ofstream
#include <ostream> // std::ostream
```
No iostream. Since std::cerr is used, proper include is <iostream>. The instruction "new includes go with the existing include block, grouped the way the file already groups them". Adding `<iostream> // std::cerr` alphabetically before fstream? Group is one block sorted alphabetically: fstream, ostream. Add iostream between fstream and ostream. That maintains sorted order. Does it count as drive-by? It's needed for std::cerr. LOG_VERBOSE already used std::cerr without it, but adding is correct. Hmm, but guidance says keep diff focused; adding an include to support new code is fine. Actually <ostream> may not declare std::cerr. The fact it compiles is due to transitive includes from core/options.h. I'll add <iostream> to be correct. But wait, will clang-format complain? No.

Hmm, but would adding iostream cause a difference vs upstream? Not important. Let's add it since we now reference std::cerr explicitly in new code (already did in LOG_VERBOSE though). Actually to keep minimal, maybe don't add. The convention in logger.h uses only fstream/ostream comments. I think adding `<iostream> // std::cerr` is the right thing and "new includes go with the existing include block". The spec explicitly mentions includes, suggesting an include is expected (for files needing logger.h, and maybe iostream in logger.h). Hmm, "new includes go with the existing include block, grouped the way the file already groups them" likely refers to adding `#include "logger.h"` to command_bundle.cc and adjusting `<iostream>` comments in files where std::cerr usage is removed.

For command_bundle.cc currently `#include <iostream> // std::cout` — after removing std::cerr, std::cout remains, so comment stays fine.

For command_lint.cc `#include <iostream> // std::cerr, std::cout` — now std::cerr no longer used (line 32 was LOG_VERBOSE, doesn't count as std::cerr; actually there's no other std::cerr in command_lint.cc besides that warning). Let me check: grep command_lint for std::cerr. Only line 10 include? Let me verify. Earlier grep showed command_lint.cc:32 warning and :10 include. So after conversion, std::cerr no longer used in command_lint.cc. Should update comment to `// std::cout`? Check if std::cout used. Let me grep.

For resolver.h: `#include <iostream>    // std::cerr` — after conversion, std::cerr still used? The converted code uses LOG_WARNING() which returns std::cerr but doesn't name std::cerr. Other std::cerr in resolver.h? grep showed only lines 99-102. So comment could become stale. Hmm. But changing include comments is arguably part of focused diff. Upstream likely adjusted comments. But careful: resolver.h uses std::cerr nowhere else? Let me check. grep std::cerr resolver.h gave lines 25 include, 99,101,102. So after conversion, no std::cerr. But `#include <iostream>` might still be needed for other iostream things (std::ostream?). Let me grep for cout/endl etc.

For command_validate.cc: std::cerr used many places (print functions, fail output), so include comment stays.

Let me grep each file.
